hook.line: Vale wants to know when Tomás will ring her about Simón. He can say it two ways, and to a Bogotano they don't sound the same: one is a plan, the other is a promise.
hook.en: I'm going to call you tomorrow.

examples.en: I'm going to call you tomorrow.
What are you going to do on Saturday? (to a friend)

examples.es: Vamos a buscar a Simón en el parque.
examples.en: We're going to look for Simón in the park.

examples.es: Mañana lloverá en toda la ciudad.
examples.en: Tomorrow it will rain across the whole city.

examples.es: Altamira abrirá una oficina en el barrio.
examples.en: Altamira will open an office in the neighbourhood.
Don't worry, everything will turn out fine. (to a man)

rule:
Both forms talk about the future, but they live in different places.

*Voy a* plus an infinitive is the everyday one. Plans, intentions, what you're up to this weekend: *¿Qué vas a hacer el sábado?* *Vamos a buscar a Simón.* In conversation this is your default, and you'll rarely sound wrong with it.

The *-ré* form carries a little weight. Use it for:
promises: *Te llamaré.*
forecasts: *Mañana lloverá.*
the news and formal plans: *Altamira abrirá una oficina.*
comfort and big statements: *Todo saldrá bien.*

A rough English guide: *voy a* is going to, and *-ré* is will, said like you mean it. A friend asking about your weekend gets *voy a*. A friend you've let down gets *te llamaré, te lo prometo*.

One thing never changes: after *voy a*, the verb stays in its dictionary form.
smallPrint: Teachers call these the periphrastic future (*ir a* plus infinitive) and the simple future (*futuro simple*).

yourTurn.prompt: A friend asks about your Saturday. Pick *voy a trabajar* or *trabajaré* and type the whole sentence: *El sábado ___.* (On Saturday I'm going to work.)
yourTurn.why: A plan in a chat between friends: *voy a*.

yourTurn.prompt: You're reading the weather on the news. Pick *va a llover* or *lloverá* and type the whole sentence: *Mañana ___ en Bogotá.* (It will rain in Bogotá tomorrow.)
yourTurn.why: Forecasts on the news use the *-ré* future.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: What are you going to do this weekend?
yourTurn.answer: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
accept: ¿Este fin de semana qué vas a hacer?
yourTurn.why: Asking about plans is *voy a* territory.

yourTurn.prompt: Promise Vale: I'll call you tomorrow.
Comfort Tomás: Don't worry, everything will turn out fine.
accept: Tranquilo, todo va a salir bien.
yourTurn.why: Comfort is a big statement, so *saldrá* fits; *va a salir* is fine too.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn the plan into a promise: *Te voy a ayudar.* (I'll help you.)
yourTurn.why: Drop *voy a* and put the ending on the verb: *ayudaré*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make the forecast casual, the way you'd say it to a friend: *Mañana lloverá.* (It's going to rain tomorrow.)
yourTurn.why: In a chat, *va a* plus the dictionary form *llover*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After *voy a* the verb stays in its dictionary form; it's one future or the other, never both.
Don't drop the little *a*: it's *va a* plus the infinitive.
Not wrong, just stiff. Between friends, plans take *voy a*.

personal: Write two lines about next week: one plan with *voy a*, and one promise to someone with a *-ré* verb.
